segmenti.tekst: نحن نقص عليك أحسن القصص بما أوحينا إليك هذا القرآن وإن كنت من قبله لمن الغافلين. الحمد لله رب العالمين، والصلاة والسلام على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وصحبه أجمعين. After Yusuf's brothers came to Egypt together with Benjamin and entered upon Yusuf in his residence, Yusuf took his brother Benjamin aside and embraced him.
He embraced him tightly and said to him: "I am your brother, I am your brother Yusuf, and do not, do not be sad about what they did to me, or to us: to me, to you, to our father."

After that Yusuf, alayhis-salam (peace be upon him), informed his brother of what he wanted to do, so that his brother Benjamin would remain in Egypt. So he took the vessel from which the king drank. That is, the king had given that vessel to them so that they could scoop up the food with it, that wheat, and thus measure the food.

The king had given it out of kindness, out of respect. It is said that it was golden; that is why it was so valuable and that is why they stopped the whole caravan. So, it says, Yusuf ordered his servants to put that vessel into their load, but not into their load as such, but into the load of his brother Benjamin.

And then, when they set off to leave the city, a herald cried out, saying: "O you of the caravan, come back, you are thieves!" So they came back and said: "What do you mean, thieves? We are not thieves," and so on, and so on.
And then what follows? Yusuf orders his servants to search that caravan. Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, says: "فَبَدَأَ بِأَوْعِيَتِهِمْ قَبْلَ وِعَاءِ أَخِيهِ" – He says: so this inspector began…

Some say it was Yusuf, but Allah knows best, because Yusuf was a ruler; it does not befit Yusuf to go searching and rummaging through things; rather, Yusuf was present, but he ordered the inspector to search the things.

See, it says: "fa bada'a bi aw'iyatihim" – so, it says, the inspector began to search first through their belongings, that is, the belongings of these ten brothers. Because had he begun first with Benjamin's belongings, it would already have been exposed, it would have been transparent; they would immediately have said: "This is some trick." But Yusuf arranged it so that they would not sense that it was a set-up or some trick on Yusuf's part.
So, it says, it went one by one. And every time, it says, whenever they finished one of those camel-loads, they would say: "There, you see that we are telling the truth.
You see, there's nothing." And every time, it says, this would increase their confidence. It says: and in the end they took the king's vessel out of Benjamin's camel-load.

Interestingly, here the Qur'an mentions the word "istakhraja", which means "to take out", and not "wajada", which means "they found". And how precisely the Qur'an speaks! Had the Qur'an said, that is, had the Qur'an mentioned "wajada", then it would be "they found", and then it would mean that Benjamin had stolen it.

But here the Qur'an clearly indicates to us that this was not theft, but rather Yusuf's strategy. So it says, [unclear], it says, that vessel from Benjamin's, that is, he took it out of Benjamin's, out of Benjamin's camel-load.

"Thummastakhrajaha min wi'a'i akhih. Kadhalika kidna li Yusuf, ma kana liya'khudha akhahu fi dinil-maliki illa an yasha'allah." And He says: thus We, He says, taught Yusuf that strategy, that stratagem, so that he could take his brother, which he could not have done had they judged by the law of the king of Egypt.

And we have already often mentioned that in the law, or in the sacred law of Yaqub, it was so that when a thief steals something and is then found out, he becomes the property, or the slave, of the one from whom the thing was stolen.

So Yusuf, since they had put it nicely to these men – and they were sure, as in "we did not steal" – "Fine, if you did not steal, then what is the punishment for one who steals?" They say: "He becomes the property of the one from whom the thing was stolen."

So Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, says: We, He says, taught Yusuf here this stratagem, how his brother could remain in Egypt. And his brother, that is Benjamin, knew all about it. What do his brothers say?

They say: "Well, if this Benjamin stole…" – but listen, he is not our full brother, he is, they say, a half-brother; they wanted, you know, to diminish Benjamin's worth – they say: "But you should know," they say, "his brother was also a thief" – about Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam.

They say: "If he stole," they say, "his brother was also a thief." And the scholars explain why they said that Yusuf was a thief. Some mention, it is said, that when Yusuf was little, he was, it is said, with his grandfather. And that grandfather of his on his mother's side, Rahil's side, was a polytheist.

And, it is said, Yusuf stole that idol, broke it and threw it away. Others say that he was, it is said, with his maternal aunt when his mother passed away. And his aunt, it is said, loved him very much. And when the time came for Yusuf to leave his aunt and go to Yaqub, his aunt put, it is said, this belt, some valuable belt, around his waist, and then said to Yaqub: "I cannot find that belt anywhere, and it is very valuable. So what, what should I do?

I have searched everywhere." And, it is said, in front of Yaqub she uncovered this child and said: "There it is," she says, "he stole," she says, "that valuable belt of mine. And now he is my slave." And we said, well, that according to the sacred law of Yaqub, whoever stole something became the slave of the one from whom the thing was stolen. And, it is said, he stayed with her until she passed away, and after that Yaqub took him. But Allah knows best, none of this is so, that is, these narrations are not correct; these are Isra'iliyyat. That is what came to us from the Children of Israel (Banu Isra'il).

So, Allah knows best, [unclear] opinion, and the most correct is that they lied about Yusuf. They lied about Yusuf, just as they had lied before. So they say: "He is a thief." It says: "Fa asarraha Yusufu fi nafsihi."

So, it says, Yusuf did not want… it hurt him that they lied about him. But, it says, he kept it hidden within himself; he did not want to tell them there, in that place: "You are liars, you did this and that to me, to my father, to my brother," and so on. It says: so, it says, he hid it – what did he hide?

He says: "You are in a worse position, for you are what you describe us as, and Allah knows best what you describe us as." And, it says, after that they began to address Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam, ingratiatingly, in order to soften his heart so that he would release Benjamin. It says: "Qalu ya ayyuhal-'azizu inna lahu aban shaykhan kabiran fa khudh ahadana makanahu, inna naraka minal-muhsinin."

They say: "O you, prime minister" – let us put it that way, since Yusuf was at that time in the position of, let's say, prime minister, the second man in the state – they say: "Benjamin has an old father, who will not be able to bear being separated from him.

He will not be able to bear it. He is old, frail, weakened; it will hit him hard. Perhaps he won't even survive when he hears it." They say: "So take one of us in his place." What does Yusuf say to them?
He says: "Far be it, Allah forbid," he says, "that we take someone in his place. Far be it that we take anyone other than the one with whom we found this vessel.
If we did that," he says, "we would be wrongdoers." It would be an injustice: how could we take an innocent man as a slave and let this one, in quotation marks, thief walk free?

No, no. So they began to plead with him there, to ask for him, etc. The Qur'an says further: and when they could not convince him in any way, they lost all hope, it says, and withdrew to talk, to consult one another about what to do. What does one of them, that is, the eldest brother, say to them? And their eldest brother said, it says: "Did your father not
take a pledge from you that you would bring Benjamin back to him? Isn't that so?" They say: "It is." "And," he says, "before that you went too far with regard to Yusuf."

Now someone may ask how he can say to them "you went too far with regard to Yusuf" when he himself took part in it. This was, Allah knows best, the brother who said: "La taqtulu Yusufa wa alquhu fi ghayabatil-jubb" – he says: do not kill Yusuf, that is going too far, but rather, he says, throw him into the well. And, it is said, this is the same brother who, let's say, in a way saved Yusuf, alayhis-salatu was-salam, from death, so that his brothers would not

kill him. It says [unclear], and he says to them: "And before," he says, "you went too far," he says, "with regard to Yusuf." He says: "وَلَنْ أَبْرَحَ الْأَرْضَ حَتَّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أَبِي" – he says: "And I will not leave," he says, "Egypt. I don't have," he says, "the face to appear before my father, until my father permits me" – to return to Palestine – "aw yahkumallahu li" – "or until Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, decides for me" – that he come with his brother to Palestine – "and truly He is the best, the best", that is, the best of those who judge, who judge.

Here we will, in sha Allah, stop, and tomorrow, in sha Allah, we will continue further. There is not much left of this surah, just a little more is left. We are already nearing the end, and we are also nearing the end of the month, the month of Ramadan. And a person should make the most, the most of these last days, dear brothers.

It is interesting that we have introduced praying eight rak'ahs – which is sad – but again people, well… the mosque is full at the beginning, and already people start leaving after the fourth rak'ah. Which is not… let's say, one can find some excuse, dear brothers, for a person to say after eight rak'ahs: "Well, let's go, it's from the Sunnah."

But for a person to leave after four rak'ahs – meaning, that is really already… that already goes against the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him). Meaning, that is already… that already goes against the Sunnah of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam. Also, regarding these even and odd nights, it is the same as a student who crams right before the exam and wants to pass the exam.

It happens, he may pass the exam, but how much knowledge he has, Allah knows best. And it may happen, dear brothers… if we go by the Saudi calculation, meaning, tonight was an odd night. If we go by ours, then tomorrow is an odd night. So, dear brothers, there are, meaning, quite a few tricky things here, and a person should, meaning, if he does something… the best Muslim is the one who, when he does something, does it, as our elders say, does it properly, does it well. And that is why a person should make an effort, and none of it is hard. It is not hard at all for a person to stay

after those four rak'ahs, to stay and pray four more rak'ahs. Or to come – meaning, since he already comes on the odd nights – to come on the even nights as well; 45 minutes won't hurt him. So a person should make an effort, and, by God, it is not easy to reach Jannah (Paradise) either, because the road to Jannah is full of, let's say, obstacles and thorns, while the road to Jahannam (Hellfire) is easy, all enjoyment, all desires. That is why a person should be careful and mindful. May Allah grant you every good. Wa sallallahu 'ala nabiyyina Muhammadin
wa 'ala alihi wa sahbihi. Was-salamu alaykum.
